stem: X, who was not in danger of death, disappeared at the age of 76. It being unknown whether or not he still lives, he shall be presumed dead for purposes of succession after an absence of:
explanation: Art. 390, 2nd par.: 'If he disappeared after the age of seventy-five years, an absence of five years shall be sufficient in order that his succession may be opened.'

stem: X, in danger of death, disappeared at the age of 76. It being unknown whether or not he still lives, he shall be presumed dead for purposes of succession after an absence of:
explanation: Art. 391(3): a person in danger of death whose existence has not been known for four years is presumed dead for all purposes, including the division of the estate. Age is irrelevant in Art. 391.

stem: X, who was not in danger of death, disappeared at age 69. It being unknown whether or not he lives, he is presumed dead for succession after an absence of:
explanation: Art. 390, 2nd par.: ten years (he was not over 75).

stem: The absentee shall not be presumed dead for the purpose of opening his succession till after an absence of ten years.
explanation: Keyed FALSE. The sentence copies Art. 390, 2nd par., but drops the rest: five years suffice if he disappeared after 75, and four years under Art. 391 if he disappeared in danger of death. Sir's 'absolutely true' standard makes it false.
key_note: Keyed FALSE although it copies the first sentence of Art. 390, 2nd par.

stem: Two years having elapsed without any news about the absentee or since the receipt of the last news, and five years in case the absentee has left a person in charge of the administration of his property, his absence may be declared.
The judicial declaration of absence shall take effect upon its publication in a newspaper of general circulation.
explanation: Art. 386: not until SIX MONTHS after its publication.

stem: The relatives or friends of the absentee may ask for the declaration of absence.
explanation: Art. 385 lists: (1) the spouse present, (2) the heirs instituted in a will, (3) the relatives who may succeed by intestacy, (4) those with a right over his property subordinated to his death. A FRIEND may only ask for a provisional representative (Art. 381).

stem: After an absence of seven years, it being unknown whether or not the absentee still lives, he shall be presumed dead for all purposes.
explanation: Art. 390: 'for all purposes, EXCEPT for those of succession.'

stem: A person on board a vessel lost during a sea voyage, who has not been heard of for four years since the loss of the vessel, shall be presumed dead for all purposes except the division of his estate.
explanation: Art. 391: 'for all purposes, INCLUDING the division of the estate among the heirs.'

stem: If the absentee appears, he shall recover his property in the condition in which it may be found, together with its fruits and rents.
explanation: Art. 392: 'but he cannot claim either fruits or rents.'

stem: The wife appointed administratrix of her absent husband's property may alienate or encumber it in the course of administration.
For the spouse present to remarry, how long must the absent spouse have been missing under ordinary circumstances (no danger of death)?
explanation: FC 41: four consecutive years and a well-founded belief of death, plus a summary judicial declaration of presumptive death; two years if there was danger of death under Art. 391.

stem: Which statement on the declaration of absence is correct?
choices: Only the spouse may ask for it
It is always required before a spouse may administer the absentee's property, in a separate prior case
It is needed when the absentee has property to be administered, and the petition may be combined with one for administration
It is needed merely to establish the fact of absence
explanation: Reyes v. Alejandro; Tol-Noquera v. Villamor; Peyer v. Martinez. The rules protect the absentee's property, not the administrator.

stem: The ship's last messages reported that it was sinking and the crew abandoning ship; nothing more was heard. Two months later, the captain's wife claims his monthly allotments, arguing he cannot be presumed dead until four years pass. Is she right?
choices: No, because seven years are required
No; where facts lead to a moral certainty of death, the presumption yields to the preponderance of evidence, so she gets death benefits instead
Yes, until a court declares him dead
explanation: Eastern Shipping Lines v. Lucero (1983), citing Joaquin v. Navarro.

stem: X disappeared in 1940. Y died in 1942 instituting X as heir. In 1950 X's children claim the inheritance. What must they prove?
choices: Nothing; the presumption of death suffices
That X was alive when Y died in 1942
explanation: Art. 393: whoever claims a right of a person whose existence is not recognized must prove that he was living when his existence was necessary to acquire it.
